Reduction of Have in Past Modals and in Auxiliary Verbs

When you use auxiliary verbs like have, it is common to reduce it in speaking.

In English, not every word or syllable is fully pronounced.

When you reduce the sound of have it sounds like uv or iv.

Read each sentence in it's full form:

• Most kids in the U.S. could have spent up to five hours in front of the television today.
  • If there are no parent controls on the TV they could have been watching anything!
  • They feel that the first priority of cartoons and kids' shows should have been to educate, not to sell merchandise.
  • He or she would have witnessed 8,000 murders and over 100,000 other acts of violence.
  • By the time that child is 18 years of age, he or she might have witnessed 200,000 acts of violence.
  • So, parents who think that much content should have been reserved for late night television are right.
  • They might have also realized that violence is visible in newscasts.
Now read them and reduce the pronunciation of the auxiliary verb have:

• Most kids in the US could've spent up to five hours in front of the television today. could_uv
  • They feel that the first priority of cartoons and kids' shows should've been to educate, not to sell merchandise. should_uv
  • He or she would've witnessed 8,000 murders and over 100,000 other acts of violence. would_uv
  • By the time that child is 18 years of age; he or she might've witnessed 200,000 acts of violence. might_uv
  • So, parents who think that much content should've been reserved for late night television are right. should_uv
  • They might've also realized that violence is visible in newscasts. might_uv
Tonic, Contrastive, Emphatic and New Information Stress

There are various types of stress used when speaking English.
Sentence stress gives English its rhythm or "beat".
Tonic stress refers to the syllable in a word which receives the most stress in an intonation unit.

For example:
  • If there are no parent controls on the TV/ they could've been watching anything!
  • What they see/ can have a strong effect on them.
  • Could it be time/ to unplug the set altogether?
When you want to point out the difference between one point and another, you use contrastive stress.

For example:
  • Other parents are concerned about the amount of violence on television.
  • The connection between media violence and aggressive behavior in real life is well documented.
  • A paper by the American Psychiatric Association on media violence has declared that to argue against that connection is like arguing against gravity.

To emphasize a word, you can change the stress from the principal word or phrase to another content word or phrase. By choosing a word other than the one you normally stress, you put emphasis on the new one.

For example:
  • It's not surprising that more and more parents are becoming concerned about what their children watch.
  • Parents of younger children feel that children's programs are nothing more than commercials for toys and other products.
  • They feel that the first priority of cartoons and kids' shows should've been to educate, not to sell merchandise.

images.text:
Most kids in the US could have spent up to five hours in front of the television today. If there is no parent controls on the TV they could've been watching anything! What they see can have a strong effect on them.

It's not surprising that more and more parents are becoming concerned about what their children watch. Parents of younger children feel that children's programs are nothing more than commercials for toys and other products. They feel that the first priority of cartoons and kids' shows should've been to educate, not to sell merchandise.

Other parents are concerned about the amount of violence on television. It's estimated that by the time the average child left elementary school, he or she would've witnessed 8,000 murders and over 100,000 other acts of violence.  By the time that a child is 18 years of age; he or she might've witnessed 200,000 acts of violence, including 40,000 murders.

The connection between media violence and aggressive behavior in real life is well documented. A paper by the American Psychiatric Association on media violence has declared that to argue against that connection is like arguing against gravity.

So, parents who think that much content should've been reserved for late night television are right. They might've also realized that violence is visible in newscasts as well and saved that for late night viewing as well. Could it be time to unplug the set altogether?
